text.p: Following are some of the major events to have occurred on July 15th in history.
1099 - The crusaders captured Jerusalem, restoring the Holy City to Christendom.
1410 - Polish King Ladislas II, aided by Bohemian mercenaries, scored an overwhelming victory against the Teutonic Knights at the first Battle of Tannenberg.
1573 - The founder of classical English architecture, Inigo Jones, born. He was surveyor-general of royal buildings and also laid out Covent Garden and Lincoln's Inn Fields.

1606 - Rembrandt, Dutch painter and one of the great masters, born in Leyden as Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Rijn. Although some of his early work was unpopular at the time, he went on to produce over 650 oil paintings and 2,000 drawings.
1795 - La Marseillaise was officially adopted as the French national anthem. It was written in 1792 by Rouget De Lisle.
1815 - Napoleon surrendered to Captain Maitland of the Bellerophon at Rochefort. He was later taken into exile on St Helena.
1857 - During the Indian Mutiny, a massacre took place at Cawnpore, a frontier station. British troops and families were killed and their bodies thrown into a well.
1865 - Viscount Northcliffe born as Alfred Harmsworth in Dublin. He became a pioneer of mass circulation newspapers and later published the Daily Mirror, Daily Mail and The Times.
1869 - Margarine was patented in France by Hippolyte Mege Mouries.

1881 - William Bonney, known as "Billy The Kid", was shot dead by Sheriff Pat Garrett in New Mexico while trying to escape. Doubts surfaced about the identity of the person shot, and one story has it the real outlaw changed his name to Bushy Bill Roberts and survived until 1950.
1883 - Charles Stratton, renowned U.S. midget showman better known as General Tom Thumb, died.
1904 - Russian playwright Anton Chekhov, author of "The Three Sisters" and "The Cherry Orchard", died.
1918 - The second Battle of the Marne started when General Ludendorff launched an all-out offensive in a last-ditch attempt to overwhelm the allies.
1919 - Iris Murdoch, one of the foremost novelists of her generation, born in Dublin.
1929 - Austrian author and librettist Hugo von Hofmannstahl died. He was best known for his collaboration with composer Richard Strauss for whom he wrote the libretto to "Der Rosenkavelier".
1933 - Internationally famous classical guitarist and lutenist Julian Bream born.
1945 - Muroran, a steel centre in Japan, was shelled by the U.S. Third Fleet in the closing stages of World War Two.
1953 - John Christie, murderer of at least six women at Ten Rillington Place, London, was hanged.
1960 - France agreed to grant independence to Gabon, effective from August.
1964 - Anastas Mikoyan succeeded Leonid Brezhnev as President of the Soviet Union.
1965 - The Mariner IV spacecraft launched in November 1964 sent back the first close-up pictures of Mars.
1968 - The first direct air services between the U.S. and the Soviet Union began between New York and Moscow, operated by Aeroflot and Pan American.
1974 - In Cyprus, President Makarios was overthrown in a coup led by Greek officers in the National Guard. Nikos Sampson, a former EOKA leader, was appointed president.
1983 - Six people died and 48 were injured when Armenian terrorists bombed a Turkish Airlines desk at Orly airport, Paris.
1991 - Western troops completed their pullout from Kurdish refugee havens in Northern Iraq.
1994 - European Union leaders picked Luxembourg Prime Minister Jacques Santer to head the European Commission, replacing Jacques Delors.
